tweets.text:
one of the hardest things to do in product is to slow down to speed up.

say a team has been in a perpetual whiplash mode for a year, and someone says "lets stop everything, and re-establish flow with some super small bets, even if ppl are idle for a bit"

right call, but (1/n)

...It feels like giving up. The team has likely become accustomed to -- and acclimatized to -- high WIP and chaos.

The adrenaline is overwhelming. It actually gets VERY uncomfortable to slow down...

It feels like wasteful! Your body rejects it.

Also...(2/n)

...when you hit these points, someone invariably proposes that you need to revisit the "big picture".

The reset becomes about planning out another big batch of work, and creating a sense of certainty.

So instead of regaining flow...(3/n)

...you just launch back into another version of the mess you started with. You don't address the issue.

But this makes sense on the surface as well. Why do "wasteful" small work that maybe isn't the highest priority work just for the sake of getting your footing?

So...(4/n)

...we always rationalize that we can somehow regain team health and flow by just slightly re-proportioning our energy expenditure.

"10% technical debt, folks!"

No one can stomach stopping BAU.

But it is exactly what you need to do...(5/n)

The lesson.

When things have gone off the rails, resist the temptation to invent certainty and artificially reset. Resist the temptation to do "10% time".

Rather...clear the decks. Work super small. Regain momentum and confidence.

6/end
